utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the Registrar to call out the case number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13-AT, the Prosecutor versus Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the appearances please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi, Ms. Sutherland and Mr. Vos for the Prosecution, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am Tihomir Fila and together with Ms. Lopicic and Mr. Petrovic I am representing the accused. With your permission, your Honour, I have brought the report that you have requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We got it and we are grateful to you. I understand the Prosecution is going to call a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, I call Mark Crawford Wheeler. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Dr. Wheeler, may I ask you to make the solemn declaration pursuant to rule 90(b)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you to state your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Mark Wheeler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit. Dr. Wheeler, before we start with the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution, may I say that we did receive your written statement which has been read by the court, so this will enable us to be aware of what you stated in that particular document, and therefore, I wonder whether we might try to focus on events -- on the events which occurred in 1991. I do not want, of course, to constrain the Prosecution. The Prosecution may have other questions, but I just wanted to emphasise that the main concern of the court is for events which happened in 1991. The Prosecutor may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. Dr. Wheeler, you are a historian currently employed as Head of Division of Humanities in the School of European and International Studies at the University of Derby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You were educated at the University of Michigan in the United States, and then you did a PhD at the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You lectured at the in Yugoslav Studies at the University of Lancaster between 1975 and 1983.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in 1983 did you move to the School of Slovonic and East European Studies at the University of London, where you taught modern, eastern European, Balkan and Yugoslav history until 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And has your scholarly research and publications centred on Yugoslavia, especially during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you appointed by the British Cabinet Office to write the official history of the Special Operations Executive in wartime Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1994 did you become Programme Manager for the Former Yugoslavia with the charity "Help Aid International"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in 1996 did you become project director in Sarajevo Institute of War and Peace Reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In March 1997 did you become Chair of the Media Experts Commission established by the Joint Implementation Committee on Elections in the United Nations Transitional Administration in Eastern Slavonia, Birinja and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In addition to the three years you spent working in the former Yugoslavia, have you lived and studied in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you visited one or more of the Yugoslavia Republics at least twice each year since 1969?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you speak the Yugoslavia language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I speak Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, is your evidence based upon your personal knowledge and drawn from your own work and that of other recognised scholars in this field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you based your research on conversations with knowledgeable persons and documents made available to you by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And since 1980 have you published numerous books and articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at the curriculum vitae that is now handed to you and can you confirm that this is your curriculum vitae? (Handed)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, if your Honours please. Might it be marked with the first exhibit number of the Prosecution? Is that acceptable to your Honour? Okay. Dr. Wheeler, having regard to what his Honour said about moving as quickly as possibly we can to the events in 1991, I would just ask you if, briefly, you can tell us, was there any ethnic persecution adopted by the participants in the Second World War in the former Yugoslavia in this particular area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there certainly was. It was notable that what took place during the Second World War in Yugoslavia was unique in terms of the scale and the ferocity of the carnage. South Slavs had occasionally fought each other before 1941, but never on the scale that took place in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the approach of the Yugoslavia Communists to the national question during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Yugoslavia Communist Party sought to use the national question as one of the vehicles by which they both pursued a successful resistance policy and ultimately installed themselves in power and, they, contrary to the failures of their rivals and opponents, actually made the national question one of the most successful of the planks that they offered in order to achieve power.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe the nature of the ethnic violence during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the precipitating event in terms of the violence amongst south Slavs was the German installation in power in Zagreb of the Ustasha terrorist organisation. The Ustasha was a fascist outfit which had been founded in 1929, had been patronised principally by Italy and Hungary before the Second World War, but then was put in power by Hitler, and the Ustashe under Ante Pavelic determined very soon after achieving power in April 1941 that it was going to ethnically purify Croatia, doing so by expelling roughly a third of the Serb or other so-called "Oriental" parts of the population, converting a third of the Serb minority to Roman Catholicism and simply butchering the remaining third, and this actually set in motion what became a rather more widespread series of persecutions and reprisals amongst the south Slav peoples, but the motor force came from the Ustasha policy of genocide in the vastly expanded war-time Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did the Communists deal with the legacy of the fracticidal strife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after the Second World War the Communist line was that what had happened in terms of internecine strife in the course of the Second World War had really been entirely the fault of the occupying powers, or of their lackeys amongst the old order, the respective bourgeoisies of the Serbs, Croats, Slovenians and so forth, and as a consequence it had nothing to do with them and nothing to do with the new workers' state that was in the process of formation. So, by and large what the Communists did was to try and draw a line under what had happened in the Second World War and caused people, to the maximum possible extent, to forget it. Later on this, of course, would be seen as having been something of a mistake because there was no process of expurgation or reconciliation following the war. There was -- people felt that they somehow were being forced to forgive and forget in a way which left some of their wounds untreated, unbound-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did Tito set up his constitutional structure after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Yugoslavia Communists had a very definite model in mind, ever since the early years of the 19th century, Stalin, who was supposed to be the great communist expert in national question matters, had decreed that multinational states should be national in form but socialist in content. What this meant in the case of the Yugoslavia Communists coming to power in 1944 was that they had a ready-made model in front of them in the federal structure of the Soviet Union. Of course, in other words, the Republics and autonomous provinces were effectively decorative in function, the party had no intention whatsoever of relinquishing its monopoly of power, but the national particularities, the national sensibilities of the various peoples in Yugoslavia, as had been the case earlier in the Soviet Union, was to be massaged or otherwise propitiated by the manufacture of a spurious federalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did the federal Yugoslavia structure change over the years from World War II?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, contrary to what either the Yugoslavia Communists, or Stalin for that matter, had envisaged, instead of things working out according to the foremost architectural principle of function following form, in fact in Yugoslavia it worked the other way around and form followed function. That is, the various Republics over the years, contrary to Communist expectations, acquired more and more effective power, more and more autonomy. Their respective republican Communist parties became more and more inclined to look upon the other Communist parties as rivals, and this was a process which effectively began in the early 1960s and was then consummated in the 1974 constitution which in many respects turned the Yugoslav Federation into what amounted to a confederation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Wheeler, when you are speaking would you kindly speak as slowly as you possibly can because the interpreters have to translate into a number of languages and they have a very difficult task. If you can assist us by speaking slowly, we would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Wheeler, you mentioned the 1974 constitution. Did this constitution have any effect on the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the early 1970s the national question and the dangers of the national question had become so manifest that Tito had been up-lodged in the case of the so-called mass "pok" or mass movement in Croatia, to threaten the use of the army to preserve and protect the achievements of socialism, and of course guarantee the Party's monopoly of power and Party's unity. As a result of this experience in 1971/72, the 1974 constitution actually specified that the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, besides having the duty of defending the country, had the duty of defending the socio-political order, that is Communist power.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did the 1974 constitution work in practice, both before and after Tito died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, before Tito died -- I should say at the outset that one of the purposes of the 1974 constitution had been to create a system which would outlast Tito himself. In other words, it was a constitution designed to do away with the need for another Tito. It was designed to cope with the cessation and create a system that would be somehow almost a perpetual-motion machine which would be mutually self-sustaining, mutually-supporting, and it appeared, in fact, while Tito was alive, to work, but that, of course, was precisely the problem. It worked only because Tito was still alive. It worked because he was there to serve as an arbiter, as a final judge in all matters of dispute between the various Republics, between various other economic or social or geographical interest groups, and therefore, the fact that the constitution posed very basic problems was masked. Upon Tito's death, however, these problems all became obvious. The high judge rule that Tito had formerly played was no longer there, of course, the collective presidency that succeeded him almost always proved incapable of coming to any sort of effective consensus, and perhaps in some senses most importantly the good times that had characterised the 1970s in Yugoslavia, ever-rising standards of living, ever-increasing foreign borrowing, these good times came to an end and so the coincidence of Tito no longer being there to play pater familiaris or stern patriarch as required, and then the economy going bad, emphasised the failures of this, or the incapacity of this, constitutional system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Wheeler, what is the "SJMU memorandum" and what is its significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in 1986 a subcommittee of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts, that is SJMU, produced a draft memorandum effectively describing the state of Serbia. I mean that is the condition of Serbia, within the Yugoslav Federation, and bemoaning the depths to which it had fallen, bemoaning in particular the ever-greater demographic alienation of Kosovo, that is the departure of Serbs and Montenegrins and the ever-expanding Albanian majority, bemoaning the fact in which the economic system in Yugoslavia seemed to work against Serbia. In any case, this memorandum, although existing only in draft form, was published, and in a sense it came a catalyst for demonstrating how much of a sense of angst, disapproval, despair, existed amongst a significant part of the Serbian intelligentsia and therefore potentially amongst the Serbian masses as well, about the way in which Yugoslavia after Tito was moving. This demonstration of a popular mood had a profound effect on the career of one rising "aparatchnik" in the Serbian party, that is Slobodan Milosevic who, although initially condemning the SJMU memorandum did, eventually, saw the way the wind was blowing and used it effectively as a vehicle whereby he came gradually to substitute a Serbian nationalist agenda for the old socialism or communism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: To what extent did people see a relevance or legacy of the Second World War in the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as the Yugoslav Communist system atrophied, as the Cold War ended, and as events in eastern Europe -- elsewhere in eastern Europe showed what the fate of Communist regimes was likely to be, there was a general de-legitimisation or crisis of confidence, crisis of legitimacy for the Communist regime in Yugoslavia. The Serbs in particular had been spending the previous several years attacking the legacy of Tito and Tito himself. In a sense, what this meant was that people were increasingly coming to disbelieve all the old Communist orthodoxies that had prevailed and in this vacuum of belief, nationalism, as I already hinted, was becoming the new faith, but along with it was a desire to take up the national struggle that had prevailed during the Second World War. In other words, the Communists, having spent 40 years telling the people of Yugoslavia that the victory of the socialist revolution in the Second World War was the answer to all of their needs, the answer to all of their prayers, if I can even say that, there was this tendency, throughout Yugoslavia, to, in fact, embrace the devil that the Communists had previously castigated. In other words, everything that the Communists had said, even though in many cases it was in historical terms true, was disbelieved, and in this climate of Communist failure, change throughout eastern Europe, the rendering of Yugoslavia as a state ever-more insignificant because of the end of the Cold War, people in a sense abandoned their previous beliefs and looked for new ones. Well, nationalism was the new one, and the big nationalist issue, of course, was what had happened or not happened in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What brought about the downfall of the Yugoslavia Communist party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that also, of course, was tied in with the pattern of events generally in eastern Europe, but in the specific Yugoslav circumstances it all had to do with what had become the principal plank of Milosevic's rise to supremacy in Serbia, which was the so-called "reunification" of Serbia, that is getting rid of the autonomy of the formerly autonomous provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina and the way in which, in order to appease him, the other republican parties had, during 1988 and 1989, effectively conspired to let him get away with it. What this meant was that an increasingly large number of the populus in the non-Serb-controlled Republics saw what was going on with the giving-way to Milosevic as an indication of their own party's inability to defend their own republican interests. What I am trying to get around to saying, of course, is that in January 1990 at the 14th and last Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, the Slovenes first and then the Croats walked out, in a sense breaking with the Party and therefore destroying the Party, in recognition of their own previous errors in having accommodated Milosevic's drive for the re-unification of Serbia, the fear, of course in the non-Serb republics being that, "Today it is Kosovo and Vojvodina and Montenegro", tomorrow it is going to be us that are going to fall victim to Serb centralism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did Yugoslavia find itself having multi-party elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Communist parties in Slovenia and Croatia, having broken with the Federal Party, needed to achieve for themselves new democratic mandates, and so they embraced multi-party elections, fully expecting, of course, to win them, but in both cases they were mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the result of the 1990 elections in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Croatia, very much contrary to the expectation of the would-be reformed and re-named League of Communists of Croatia, a new party headed by Franjo Tudjman, that is the Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ, won the elections, not because it won an overall number of the popular votes but because the "first past the post", electoral system meant that it could win an overwhelming majority of the seats in the "Sabor", the Croatian Parliament, on something like 41 or 42 per cent of the votes. This had been a system which the Communists or the former Communists in Croatia had thought would work to their benefit. In fact, it worked to Tudjman's benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the reaction by the Serbs in Croatia to the Tudjman regime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian reaction in Croatia was one, by and large, of profound alarm. The Serb minority in Croatia, like Serbs in Bosnia or the Serbs in Kosovo, and Vojvodina before that, of course, had been profoundly affected by the whipping-up of hysteria which Milosevic had used in the late 1980s to push through what he liked to call his "anti-bureaucratic revolution", and of course the mass media based in Serbia had helped Milosevic in this regard. In fact, they had been the principal agents of his campaign of radicalising Serbs, getting Serbs terribly excited about what their likely fate would be, making them demand, whether they were in Serbia or elsewhere in Yugoslavia, some sort of effective unification, and so the advent of Tudjman to power, whose campaign rhetoric had been incautious to say the least, convinced a tremendous number of Serbs, especially those Serbs in Croatia who inhabited the rather backward, poverty-stricken rural areas who had been most greatly affected by the Ustasha genocide in the Second World War. This was sufficient to convince them, in fact, that the Ustasha was back in power and that Franjo Tudjman was no more and no better than Ante Pavelic had been in 1941.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What policies were being pursued by Slobodan Milosevic concurrent with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course what Milosevic was busy doing in 1990 and 1991 was seeking to discover how much of the Yugoslav Federation he could come to control, and the Serb minority in Croatia or the Serb minority in Bosnia, or Serbs, wherever they might be, were his vehicles for seeking to expand the realm of his power. At the same time, of course, as it becomes obvious that the game of increasing Serb power would be very more easily pursued if the Slovenes were no longer a part of the picture, Milosevic is dropping hints everywhere that Slovenia's eventual secession would be easily accommodated. At the same time, of course, Milosevic is also seeking to secure his position in what at that stage was still seen as the principal bulwark of the Yugoslav state, and that is the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the role of the Yugoslav's People's Army at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when, in the summer of 1990, popular rebellions break out in the Serb uninhabited pale of Croatia, that is areas in northern Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun, when Serb rebellions take place there, local Serb communities erecting barricades, taking over police stations, that sort of thing, the JNA is around, providing weapons, providing advice, providing encouragement. This was, at this point, probably something that did not reflect -- did not necessarily reflect -- an overall view of the high command, but it reflected the extent to which there was a growing co-mingling, a growing community of interest between the JNA and the Milosevic regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps we might, if we could, have a look at a map on the screen, B2-6, and I have a hard copy of this that I can tender too, if your Honours please. The Defence have been provided with a copy. There is a copy there for your Honours. (Map shown) Dr. Wheeler, do you recognise the map that now appears on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That is a map, although the reproduction on the video scene is not very good, which shows the pattern of Serb settlement in the Republic of Croatia. The darker blue indicates areas with Serb majorities, the lighter blue indicates areas where there are large Serbian minorities. Now, that pattern of settlement to some degree corresponds with the boundaries of the old Hapsburg military frontier, something which had been set up by the Hapsburgs, in the 15th and 16th centuries as a bastion of south-east defence against the Turks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The significant thing that should be borne in mind, however, about the map, is that the areas of Serbian absolute majorities were very sparsely populated regions, by and large, and so that in a territorial sense, the Serb-inhabited, or Serb majority-inhabited areas of Croatia were large, but in a population sense they were very small. Most Serbs lived in not in those areas but rather in Croatia's big cities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence counsel whether he objects to this map being regarded as exhibit number 2, exhibit number 1 being the statement of Dr. Wheeler. Any objection? Sorry, CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objections as to the admission of the CV of Mr. Wheeler. I have looked at the maps and they are all authentic and we accept them as such. My expert witness, an historian, will bring his maps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will have this as exhibit number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Wheeler, you touched upon the attitude of Slobodan Milosevic to cessation by Slovenia. What was his attitude to Croatian cessation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was more complicated, and it probably is safe to say that it evolved with time. Milosevic, I think, can be regarded as having -- well, in political terms, of course, Milosevic is and remains an opportunist of the highest degree, which means that he goes after whatever is possible. There may have been a time in the late 1980s when he thought he could actually Serbianise or exert control over all of the Yugoslav Federation. It became obvious, however, over the months that this was not going to be possible, and he had to accommodate himself to smaller ambitions. In a sense, ridding the Yugoslav Federation of the highly troublesome, because western-orientated, and very self-confident Slovenes, who, of course, did not have any Serbian minority on their territory, was going to make it easier to deal with the remaining Republics where there were large Serbian minorities. The principle which gradually became the dominant one as far as Milosevic was concerned was that it was fine if other Republics wanted to leave Yugoslavia, as long as they did not take any Serbs with them. So, in other words, the areas where Serbs lived must remain inside Yugoslavia. Milosevic, on the other hand, never imagined until probably late 1991, early 1992, that he was going to have any trouble convincing the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina that they should stay inside Yugoslavia. They were rather left out of his calculations until late in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your opinion, what was Milosevic's attitude -- sorry, in your opinion, was Milosevic's attitude compatible with the maintenance of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, indeed it was not. Slobodan Milosevic was the first of the secessionists in Yugoslavia. He was the first person, effectively, to embark upon destroying the Yugoslav Federation. What was too clever about his tactics is that he announced possibly, or proclaimed from every possible pulpit that he was the arch defender of Yugoslavia, when in fact ever since embarking on the destruction of Kosovo and Montenegro and Vojvodina in 1988 and 1989 he was the man who was destroying Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the progress of Croatian independence during the early part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Croats proceeded rather haltingly. On the one hand they were vastly aware of the dangers of getting out of step with the Slovenes, the Slovenes having decided in a great national referendum in December of 1990 that they would declare their independence, or rather, as they spoke at the time, "seek disassociation", from Yugoslavia, if the country were not transformed into a loose federation or a loose association of sovereign republics by June of 1991. The Slovenes rather set the agenda thereby for the Croats, and Tudjman, who came to power in April/May 1990 without any effective armed forces, not even with a police force that in fact he could trust to do his bidding, he was obliged to allow the Slovenes to set the pace. The Slovenes, on the other hand, were vastly more prepared for asserting their sovereignty than the Croats were, but the Croats, nonetheless, could not run the risk of being left out on a limb by themselves and therefore subjected, as they thought solely, to the potential opposition of the regime in Belgrade or the JNA. So they marched in step with the Slovenes, although they did not hold their independence referendum until the middle of May 1991; in other words, only just a month before the eventual declaration of independence on 25th June 1991. But it is fair to say that when Croatia declared its independence it did not know how it was going to actually make good on that declaration, unlike the Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I assume it is obvious from what you say, but what was the result of the May 1991 referendum on independence, Croatian referendum on independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The overwhelming majority of those who voted, voted in favour of independence, although again, not all the options were being excluded. The Croats, like the Slovenes before them, certainly continued to see circumstances in which a Yugoslavia reformed to their taste would be one in which it might be advantageous for them to live. This certainly was the tenor of popular opinion, both in Slovenia and Croatia. Now, Tudjman himself personally was always much more of an ardent proponent of fully-fledged independence than many other people and his Party, or for that matter, many other people in Croatia were, but he was prepared to go slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did Milosevic accept that Croatian secession was inevitable and what was his attitude to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one can cite various points at which Milosevic accepts the notion that the Croats possess the right to secede, to go their own way. He was saying rather frequently that in the early months of 1991, but of course there was always the caveat, there was always the exception. The Croats were free to go, but they were not free to take any Serb-inhabited territory with them, and of course it was up to him, that is Slobodan Milosevic and his loyal Serb followers in Croatia, at that time in Croatia in particular, if we are talking about Croatia in particular, to define what that territory was. Some of it, of course, might be thought, if you think back to that map we looked at before, as being obviously, from an ethnographic point of view, indisputably Serb, but Milosevic and his minions were not, of course, ready just to stop at that. I mean, they wanted more, and one of the most common Serb definitions of what it was they expected to get out of a Croatia that left the Yugoslav Federation was a line from Karlobag on the coast through Ogulin, Karlovac, to Virovitica near the Hungarian frontier. In other words, that would have been an amputation of a huge part of Croatia, much of which, of course, was inhabited by Croats rather than Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it perhaps might assist if you could point that out to us on a map as best you can, and if we could have on the computer screen B-1-1, and I have also copies of that which I can make available to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try this map. Is the technician capable of pointing out Karlobag? I cannot see it on my map. There is an arrow somewhere there. Oh, I did that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps we have got the arrow. If that could be just zoomed in on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly we are talking about this line here. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you could just put your pointer to it, Doctor, I will ask the assistance of the technician and see whether he could mark it for us at that point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot even read -- I cannot see the islands, unfortunately, so I cannot actually read. It is opposite the island of Pag, you will see Karlobag.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Without necessarily being too precise...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. Without being too precise, if you can see my arrow, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think you have mentioned the names of the towns which will assist us if we have to go back to look at that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. May I ask Mr. Fila whether he would object to this map being tendered as exhibit number 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have objections as to the authenticity of that. That was what Milosevic had said -- I am sorry, Seselj, not Milosevic, but that is something to be discussed later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did not actually say that Milosevic had defined this as his ideal, I said it was a common expression, and in these months of early 1991, the Serbian press was full of speculations about the extent of the territory which ought to be carved out of Croatia, and this was one of the more common, if it has to be admitted, extreme versions of what a greater Serbian state in Croatia should encompass.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are you able to agree with what Mr. Fila said, that it was one of the proponents of this view was, in fact Seselj? I am sorry, did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You were asking me -- yes, indeed, Seselj was notorious for having propagated the notion that Serbia's borders should coincide with wherever a Serb was buried. This of course gave rise at the time to lots and lots of rather amusing jokes about how great "greater Serbia" should be. Seselj, of course, was also at this time -- Seselj was effectively an ally of Milosevic, hoovering up the extreme nationalist Serb vote for his radical party that would have regarded Milosevic as a former Communist, as someone who was an anathema to them. He was a sort of a stalking horse for Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Turning now to Eastern Slavonia, what impact, if any, did the Second World War have on this region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Eastern Slavonia was contained in the Ustashe state, the independent state of Croatia, so therefore Serbs in that part of the world were subjected to many of the same persecutions as took place elsewhere in the independent Croatian state, but it should be said that it was not an area, unlike, for example, parts of north-western Bosnia or Herzegovina which were notorious for containing large numbers either of rabid Croatian nationalists, or, for that matter, extreme Serb nationalists. Given the topography of the region, in other words it being very flat, nor was there an area where there was any significant resistance activity, it was not suited to it, but on the other hand, both Eastern Slavonia and Vojvodina were certainly notable, "granaries", support bases for the partisan movement in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, following the Second World War, was there a German population resident in this part of Eastern Slavonia and if so, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Banat, Backa and Eastern Slavonia had, together, a German minority of some half million persons before the Second World War. At the end of the war that German minority either fled or later was expelled on the same pattern as, of course, happened in large parts elsewhere in eastern Europe, the so-called Sudeten Germans in Czechoslovakia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And after they left, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this was significant because it freed-up large amounts of extremely fertile land and prosperous villages for resettlement by impoverished Yugoslavs from the "dinorek" or so-called passive regions of the country. This meant in the particular instance of Eastern Slavonia that large numbers of Serbs from northern Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun, came into Eastern Slavonia and large numbers of Croats from Herzegovina came in and these were people who, contrary to the equanimity or almost sort of political passivity which was notable in these sort of "fat" regions of Yugoslavia, these were people who tended towards more political zealotry, and certainly many commentators appear to think that interethnic relations, particularly relations between Serbs and Croats, were adversely affected by the arrival of these "mountain men" and their families after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is the, or what was the ethnic composition of the Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the 1991 census, the Vukovar municipality had a population of a little over 84,000. 43.7 per cent of these were Croats, 37.4 per cent were Serbs, 7.3 per cent were Yugoslavs by declaration, and the ethnic complexity, continuing ethnic complexity of the region is shown by the fact that the "others" figure is is 11.6 per cent, "others", being Muslims, Hungarians Ruthenes, Slovaks, all manner of people such as had been planted in that part of the world by the Hapsburg monarchy in previous centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I now ask if the map B1-5 could be brought up on the screen, and I also have copies of this map to make available to your Honours, and I seek to tender it as well. Again, it is a map which has been provided to the Defence. Perhaps you might just show it to Mr. Fila, just to confirm that it is the one he has. (Handed) Might it be marked, "Exhibit 4", "P4"? Mr. Fila -- oh, Mr. Fila consents. I tender that, your Honours. Before I do that, just looking at the map that you have now been shown; and which appears, also, on the television screen, can you tell me what that map represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is a map of Eastern Slavonia, and Western Srem, that part of Croatia. It does not actually show the municipal boundaries which is -- or perhaps it does. I cannot distinguish them, in any case. If the purpose of the question is to ask me to describe the Vukovar municipality, I suppose I could say that it was extremely large in geographical terms. All Yugoslavia municipalities tended to be physically large, even if their populations were not large, and when we talk -- when I mentioned before that Vukovar had a population of 84,000, that was the entire district, which ranged from Ilok which you will see in the far east of the map on the Danube, and the municipality extended virtually to the gates of Osijek in the north-west, so it was a considerable distance, 40 or 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Osijek is up to the north of the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you have mentioned Ilok and Osijek, Vukovar, of course, being in about the centre as the city.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how far to the west does the opstina go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Vukovar opstina goes up beyond Trpinja, if we find the main -- it goes just about up to where -- you see on the map the "klisa" is an aerodrome. In fact, that is the border of the municipality. I can now distinguish what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it encompasses villages like Trpinja, Bobota.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And if that has not been tendered, I tender that, your Honour. I tender that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This one? Yes. There was no objection from Mr. Fila, so it was -- I said probably the microphone was off, exhibit number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No objections. We received it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Wheeler, I think you have touched on this, but I think you said that the Vukovar region was, in the Yugoslav context, considered fairly prosperous. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, although it had suffered tremendously, like all of Yugoslavia had suffered from the economic whirlwind of the 1980s. It was no longer as prosperous as it had been. This, of course, was a political pre-condition for the break-up generally in Yugoslavia. This sense of break-up was all pervading.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did tensions mount in the Vukovar region and did this manifest itself in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Tensions rose in the area considerably later than they had elsewhere in the Serbian pail of settlement in Croatia. In other words, it would have been the summer of 1990 when the so-called log revolution took place in Knin, and it was not until late April, beginning of May, that actual, you know, physical violence was given expression -- this is 1991, of course, April/May 1991 -- that violence actually came to Eastern Slavonia. (12.00)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did any paramilitary groups participate in this build-up of violence and tension?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was one of the most distinguishing features about what happened in Eastern Slavonia, and that is that a goodly part of the incitement to violence came from outside. In the spring of 1991 Serbia-based paramilitary groups established themselves in various parts of the eastern Slovene area, around Vukovar, and began seeking to incite the local Serb population to put up barricades, seek to defend themselves from the supposedly rampaging hordes of Ustasha who were coming to slit their throats and generally make trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were any of these particular paramilitary groups that were there, were any of them capable of being identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh yes. In the early days there were several groups which set themselves up on the north western part of the Vukovar municipality, which seemed to have had separate identities but whose names are not subsequently notorious, and I certainly do not recall seeing them named particularly, but the two most latterly prominent paramilitary groups became established in the area, Seselj, Vojislav Seselj who we mentioned before, his so-called "White Eagles", otherwise known as Chetniks, and otherwise consciously embracing the legacy of the Serb guerrillas of the Second World War. His "White Eagles" or Chetniks set themselves up in Borovo Selo, Arkan, that is Raznjatovic’s, Arkan's Tigers set themselves up in the Danube-side town of Erdut, and of course it was not, it seems to me, co-incidental that the great outbreak of violence in Eastern Slavonia that took place on 2nd May occurred -- that is in Borovo Selo, occurred in an area where Seselj's White Eagles had established themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There was a matter which I am not sure we covered completely. I might just take you back to it for a second, if I can. You mention that Croatia declared independence on 25th June 1991; was this actually implemented at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is a highly technical legal question. Retrospectively, of course, it is obvious that it was implemented. At the time, because of the sudden arrival of the European Community Troika, and the subsequent conclusion on one of their later visits of the Brioni Agreement, early in July, the independence declarations of Slovenia and Croatia were put on ice for three months. There was a moratorium, effectively. Now, it is a question of argument whether or not their independence, therefore, was effective or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not asking you to answer the question. It is just the question of whether they were, in fact, independent. I am just asking you what the progress was. Now, just going back to where we were when you were talking of the paramilitaries being in this part -- active in this part of Eastern Slavonia, what role did the JNA play in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in Eastern Slavonia, the role of the JNA was very much clearer than it had been in other parts of Croatia earlier. The reason I say that is that the excuse or the explanation given for JNA involvement in various outbreaks of unrest in other parts of Croatia earlier had been that it was there to separate the combatants, impose peace, generally be a peace-keeping force. By the spring of 1991, when trouble comes to Eastern Slavonia, this pretence of even-handedness on the part of the JNA had really broken down, and the JNA was interposing itself not in the interests of peace so much as in the interests of the Serbian community in that part of the world. It was certainly becoming the case that the paramilitaries we talked about before were becoming integrated with and totally supported by the JNA, which was a pretty good indication of the extent to which the JNA was abandoning any notion of simply trying to keep the peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did the siege of Vukovar commence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are various dates given. Much of Vukovar, the centre city of Vukovar was largely cut off from the rest of Croatia by late July, but the actual big offensive on the city, the Croatian-controlled core of the city, began at the end of August. 25th August is the normal date provided. Some people say 19th August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the ultimate goal of the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the goal of the siege was to take Vukovar. In August the local Serb communities had declared their autonomy, in other words, created the second of the new Serb-ruled mini-states in Croatia, and Vukovar had been designated the capital of that mini-state, so taking the city was necessary for political reasons. Of course, the longer the siege lasted, the more -- in other words, the small band of Croatian defenders resisted the onslaught of the Serb JNA forces, then of course it became a matter of prestige. The city had to be taken because it had been invested. A third reason was, of course, that any further progress into Croatia, in other words any greater territorial expansion, would have to have a secure back, rear, and it was necessary to take Vukovar for sound military reasons as well as the political and prestige reasons I already indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What Serbian forces were utilised in the attack on Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A wide range of JNA and paramilitary forces took part in the battle. JNA forces coming -- commanded, of course, from Serbia, the overall command was in the hands, ultimately from October, of General Zivota Panic, who was commander of the first military district based in Belgrade, but there were also JNA units from Bosnia, even from Montenegro, involved in the battle. The normal estimate is upwards of 30,000 JNA troops and paramilitaries were involved in the siege and destruction of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were there any Territorial Defence units deployed in this attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One of the reasons why Tudjman in Croatia had found himself in such an embarrassing position from the point of view of actually asserting Croatia's independence from June 1991 is that the Territorial Defence in Croatia had been disarmed by the JNA, in the run-up to the elections in Croatia in 1990. What this meant was that the Croat elements of the Territorial Defence did not have any weapons but the JNA ultimately made sure that the Serb part of the Territorial Defence did, and so, the -- there was a residue of what used to be an old mixed Territorial Defence militia in Eastern Slavonia which had been armed by the JNA. Of course part of the core of the defenders, although they had to get weapons later in from elsewhere, they were also remnants, in some cases, of the old Territorial Defence system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the Croatian forces confronting in the Serbian forces in the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Estimates vary. There were between 1,000 and maybe as many as 1,800 Croatian defenders in Vukovar during the height of the siege. In other words, the ratio of attackers to defenders was hideously unbalanced, something like 15 to 1 against the Croat defenders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was there any particular unit, as such, or identified units of the Croatian forces that participated in defending the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were three particular elements. The first was the locally-based agglomeration of Territorial Defence and local police. The second was the newly-created Croatian National Guard, the ZNG, "Zbor Narodne Garde", which had been created in the summer of 1991. It managed to get a few units into Vukovar, and then the third element was the so-called HOS, the Croatian defence forces. They were a Croatian equivalent of the militaries we were talking about before. They were a neofascist paramilitary force which owed its allegiance to Dobroslav Paraga's Party of Right. So the exact numbers are unknown to me, certainly. In other words, the proportions, as between the HOS, that is these paramilitaries, and the locally-based defence forces and the ZNG, which was the creation of a new Croatian army. I am not terribly sure. We know that the HOS forces were the smallest component, but exactly their relationship one to another, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the JNA military campaign or the Serb military campaign in the area at the time limited only to Vukovar, the city of Vukovar, or did it include surrounding towns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly did not. It was rather more ambitious than that and this, of course, gave weight to the suggestion that the ambitions of Milosevic and the JNA extended well beyond any areas which had plausible Serb majorities or pluralities. On 25th and 26th August 1991, for example, the JNA and its paramilitary allies over-ran the whole district of Baranja. Baranja was an area that had a very small Serb population, 20, 25 per cent of the population was Serb. The bulk of the population was Croat and Hungarian. Then later on, in the autumn, they moved in on another area with a very small Serb population, which was Ilok, on the Danube. Ilok was a small town, had a Serb population of only 7 per cent or so, overwhelming majority were Croats and a large minority of Slovaks. Both these cases, that is the over-running of Baranja at the end of August and then the taking of Ilok in the middle of October, were notable because of the way in which the JNA itself implemented the policy that would be later called, "ethnic cleansing". In other words, the majority populations were simply got rid of. In the case of Baranja they were allowed to flee or encouraged to flee. In the case of Ilok, which was a small town but crowded with refugees from villages to the south-west of Ilok which had already been cleansed by the JNA, so that this town of something like 9,500 people probably had 12-15,000 crowded into it in October of 1991. The JNA simply moved in, issued an ultimatum and ultimately, the -- or largely unarmed Croat majority there, lest they be utterly disarmed and rendered powerless by the JNA, chose to accept the JNA's offer to get out and so they were bussed out by the JNA, which is an interesting example of the army itself manipulating an exercise in large-scale ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who ultimately succeeded in the siege of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, the overwhelming force of the JNA was ultimately triumphant, but it can be said quite fairly that the Serbs won the battle but lost the war. The reason being, of course, is that the scenes of the utter and total devastation of Vukovar, the barbarism of it all, combined at the same time with what was happening in Dubrovnik in the southern Adriatic, had the effect of losing the Serbs the propaganda war for the hearts and minds of the outside world, that they had previously been doing rather well in. In other words, Franjo Tudjman's new Croatian regime was very sceptically regarded in large parts of the outside world, but the heroic Croatian defence of Vukovar and the suffering that took place there was going to have the effect of making the Croats look like good guys, and the Serbs like beasts. This, of course, was, in military terms. The Serbs won, but in long-term sense, of course, they lost the propaganda war and then, of course, in 1995 this Serb creation itself, Republika Srpska Krajina, and Milosevic, contrary to what, of course, his role in the creation of this Serb state in Croatia, and Milosevic would not, in 1995, lift a finger to defend these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask Mr. Fila if he would like to start cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If possible I would like to leave it for tomorrow, if not, I am prepared to begin now. We received only half of the translation. I did not have time to advise my client of the contents of the statement. I can, of course, start today, but it would be more preferable for us to begin tomorrow, and in that way, I could advise my client of the statement of the witness. I know I too am in favour of a speedy trial, but we are dealing here with the territory where the accused is coming from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, since we still have almost one hour, we have 57 minutes, because we were expected to stop at quarter past one, I wonder whether you would be so kind as to start now, your cross-examination, for the sake of speeding up the whole trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I just wanted to know if it would be possible, but I am ready now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, in the maps that you have shown us, you have indicated how Serbs moved to the territory of Krajina in the 15th century and earlier. Was there a Croatian state in that territory at that time, or was there another state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, in theory, there was certainly a Croatian state. After 1102 that Croatian state had come under the Hungarian crown, in an exact relationship which was, of course, endlessly disputed by legal scholars then and subsequently, but yes, there was a Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But as part of the Austro-Hungarian empire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us the ratio of the population, the composition of the population at that time, the ratio between Serbs and Croats and what exactly belonged to Croatia? What regions were Croatian regions? Were there some other districts, other regions like Croatia, Dalmatia, Slavonia, or was it all called, "Croatia"? I am referring to the 15th century and later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Croatia at that time was, of course, known as the "Trijun" Kingdom of Croatia, Slovonia and Dalmatia. The coast, much of Dalmatia, of course, was under Venetian rule. The population structure at the time; it was extremely difficult to reconstruct. One of the whole purposes of creating the military frontier from the point of view of the Hapsburgs was to repopulate areas which had been depopulated by virtue of the continuous waging of war between the Hapsburgs and the Ottoman Turks over previous centuries. The idea was to plant a physical barrier of people there, both Croats and Serbs. Serbs coming from the Ottoman empire or from other parts of -- well, from the Ottoman empire, Croats being shipped in and wide numbers of people -- I mean, the variety of people that ended up being quite literally planted there as soldier colonists was extremely great.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I hear that there were also Croats there coming from the Ottoman empire. Which Croats came to Vojna Krajina, which Croats were in the area of Vojna Krajina? From which particular region did they come from? I mean, there were not only Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh no, not obviously Serbs. Croats from civil Croatia and I suspect from Bosnia as well, but I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You have the right to make assumptions, of course. After the First World War a state was established. What was the name of that state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was established on 1st December 1918.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: By the declaration of -- Corfu Declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Corfu Declaration was in 1917. That was a statement of the intent, ultimately, to form a Yugoslavia kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. What were the borders of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and were they the same as the borders that were established later on in the Tito's Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The Yugoslav state, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes came into existence in 1918 without established borders. The borders were not going to finally be established until, in fact, 1921, with the Treaty of Ripolo, which regulated the borders with Italy. The area that we are most concerned with here at this trial, Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem was also an area of dispute. It was only the southern part of Baranja, most of which of course remains in Hungary, was only acquired by the Yugoslav state after what amounted to a considerable military struggle with the Hungarian Bolshevik regime of Belakun at this time. Now, the borders that -- I assume Mr. Fila is asking me about the internal borders. Is that correct? The internal borders established --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, internal borders, of course. External borders are a different matter. There were changes and in 1945 there was a considerable change in the territory, in the region of history and so on, but I am here referring to internal borders. I would like to know when they came into existence and how.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The new Yugoslav state in 1918 was ruled by people who believed that in order to create Yugoslavs out of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, the separate national existence of people like Bosnian Muslims or Macedonians or Montenegrins was not recognised at the time, but in order to make Yugoslavs out of Serb, Croats and Slovenes, the state should have the most highly centralised form of government possible. This, after all, at the time, was established good practice in Europe. Regional autonomies, regional devolution were not considered to be good things by progressive people. The people who put together the new, 1921, Mvitodan Constitution in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, by and large adopted French precepts, and of course France was a highly centralised state. So the new Yugoslavia was divided --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the national --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the aim. It was not, unfortunately, the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did internal borders come into existence, and I am referring here to the borders of Banovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Banovina structure came into existence when King Alexander, in January 1929, established his royal dictatorship and the idea was that the Banovina, or "provinces" would be an appropriate translation in English, that the Banovina would, by -- they were all named after rivers or significant geographical features -- that they would complete the process of effacing, of getting rid of the lingering regional/national identities which the highly centralist royal regime wished to establish and so these Banovina cut across historical boundaries which had come down from the past, so they were an imposition of ideology and what was thought to be sound administrative practice upon geography and history.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that a wish of King Alexander, was that the idea of creating a Yugoslavia, one nation? Could we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It certainly was the same of King Alexander Karadjordjevic. The problem, of course, with Alexander's "jugoslavenzvo" Yugoslavism was that it was indistinguishable from his "srpstvo", from his Serbianism; at least that was the problem as far as non-Serbs were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who represented a minority. Did King Alexander say that the Yugoslav idea would be created, perpetuated through schools and military barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, but of course let me take you up on the business of minorities/majorities. All peoples in Yugoslavia after 1918 were minorities. There was never a majority. There was a plurality but never a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is a relative -- yes. Okay. So therefore, could we conclude that the idea of the creation of a Yugoslav nation -- you said that Tito's regime tried to establish that idea, so could we say that that idea actually belonged to King Alexander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not the progenitor of the notion. The idea of creating a Yugoslav nation was -- but certainly as a ruler, yes, in a sense, you could see a lineal descent, or a connection between the aims of Alexander and the aims of Tito, and that is to put the Yugoslavia state on very firm foundations by enhancing the degree to which the individual peoples embraced a Yugoslav ideology. However, Tito's notion of how one did that was rather different from Alexander's. The King had wished simply to Serbianise the population of Yugoslavia to the maximum possible extent. He was not a brutal man, whereas Tito wished to use socialism, Marxist/Leninist ideology to accomplish the creation of a new Yugoslav man and woman, but at the same time, allowing that person to also be a Serb, a Croat, a Slovene, an Albanian, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, one might put it that way. The idea of Yugoslavism, could you tell me, speaking of Tito's Yugoslavia, who declared, which nation declared themselves as Yugoslavs? The reason why I am asking this, and I am here mindful of the court's time, the reason why I am asking you is the difference in the census between 1971 and 1991, because one -- the number of Yugoslavs decreased in the meantime, so could you just explain to us what declared themselves as Yugoslavs in Tito's Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several reasons why people would opt to declare themselves as Yugoslavs. The common was simply that they were the products of mixed marriages and therefore it was not possible -- it was easier to say you were a Yugoslavian if your mother was a Muslim and your father was a Serb, for example. You mentioned 1971. This is an interesting case. The number of --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The census of 1981.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I believe that 1971 was mentioned as well, because we see an up and down. The 1971 census saw a vast increase in the number of declared Yugoslavs in the aftermath of the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia. The number of Yugoslavs in the 1981 census was also very healthy because it came immediately after Tito's death and it is extremely difficult now for citizens of the former Yugoslav Republics to remember how they wept and how terrified they were at the time of what was going to happen when Tito died. So then there is a great increase in the number of Yugoslavs. Now, by, of course, the 1991 census, we have had ten years of nationalist euphoria and the number of Yugoslavs goes right down, and this shows the extent to which, besides being a measure of the degree of mixed marriages, declaration as a Yugoslav was also a creature of political circumstance, and ideological conviction, so there were various reasons. (12.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you be more precise as to the idea of Yugoslavism? Was it more acceptable for Serbs? Could it be said that there were more Serbs who declared themselves as Yugoslavs than Croats, or Macedonians, Muslims, for that matter. Except for people coming from mixed marriages. There I completely agree with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think in statistical terms the number of Yugoslavs was overwhelmingly the result of the mixed marriage phenomenon which itself, of course, was a very healthy indicator of the degree to which the various south Slav peoples actually communicated in the most basic physical sense, but it would be fair to say, I believe, that more Serbs in most parts of the country found it easier to call themselves Yugoslavs by the end of this, the 20th century, than had been the case with other Yugoslav peoples. Now, if we are talking about the time of 1918, there were vastly more Croats than Slovenes who believed that they were Yugoslavs than there were Serbs, but by the late 20th century probably more Serbs were willing to embrace the idea of being Yugoslav than, certainly, Croats were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any problems created by other nations who claimed that the idea of Yugoslavism is just another attempt for Serbs to become even more dominant, to become the chief, the principal nation in Yugoslavia, and again I am referring to Tito's Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That was certainly the case that there were nationalists in amongst most of the south Slav peoples, who looked upon Yugoslavia as a vehicle for Serb domination. Equally, of course, there were Serbs who looked upon Yugoslavia as a vehicle for Croat domination, given the fact that Tito was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, but they did not really promote the idea that they should all become Yugoslavs. I mean, Croat nationalists did not claim that they should all become Yugoslavian Slavs. I mean, they insisted on their being Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since it is the wish of the court to speed up the trial, let me be more precise and come to the point. You spoke about Tito's regime. It is another story, but there is a question here that it is quite important. You have talked about the constitution from 1974, constitutional law and then the constitution. Let me ask you; have you read the Croatian constitution? I presume you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 1990 constitution? No, I have not read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, from 1974 when Yugoslavia transformed itself into...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have read the federal constitution of 1974. I have not read the Croatian republican constitution which came at the same time, the new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you cannot tell us which nations are constitutive nations in Croatian constitution from 1974?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh I certainly can, because this was, you know, a very important issue. The Croatian constitution prior to Franjo Tudjman said that Serbs -- Croats, Serbs and all other nations living on the -- and all the Yugoslav nations I guess it was, living on the territory of the Republic of Croatia are constituent peoples of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean that Serbs had equal rights as Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Not only did the -- were Serbs considered to be a founding nation of the Republic of Croatia, but the Croatian constitution, before Tudjman, gave equal rights to the Cyrillic alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To both nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. You spoke about the referendum organised by Croatia. Did Serbs participate in that referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not. They boycotted the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they maybe hold their own referendum in which they decided to remain within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did indeed. In August of 1990, Serbs in the then Serb-controlled parts held their own referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what did they decide on that referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as you said, Mr. Fila, they decided that they would remain inside Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did they actually disappear from the Croatian constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a complicated issue, because it became involved with Croatia's desire to get itself recognised abroad, and many changes were made in the Croatian constitution. But certainly the draft constitution which Tudjman proposes in the summer of 1990, in other words, soon after coming to power, commits the absolutely astonishing political error of demoting the Serbs from the status of a constituent nation of the Republic of Croatia into a "mere" national minority and this, of course, in Yugoslav parlance, which is highly idiosyncratic in these matters, is a big deal. It would not be regarded as something terribly important in other countries, but given the distinction that prevailed in Yugoslavia between nations and national minorities, the nations were the south Slavs, the national minorities were all non-south Slavs. The relegation to the role of a national minority was, of course, seen by Croatian Serbs as both an insult and potentially a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they become sort of alive amongst the Serbs? Did their fears become more pronounced and you probably are familiar with the case of Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, indeed. I mean, this is why I referred to the draft constitution promoted by Tudjman in the summer of 1990 as a colossal mistake, from his own point of view, because it played into the hands of the hate propaganda which had been coming out of Belgrade for some time, about Tudjman being another Ante Pavelic, another Ustasha "poglavnik", who was going to put all Serbs back in Jasenovac, or some place like it, so yes, the Serbs felt threatened. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You know, you must have read or watched something about Jasenovac. What happened in Jasenovac, during the independent state of Croatia, to Serbs? There were quite a few camps in Eastern Slavonia as well and do you know how many people died, perished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact number of people who perished at Jasenovac is not known, which has meant that it is subject to endless dispute, most of it motivated by extreme nationalist prejudice, hatred, or triumphalism. I mean, Franjo Tudjman himself is a principal example of the way in which the Croats had played a game of trying to diminish the number of victims at Jasenovac, which, of course, were not only Serbs but also Jews, gypsies and anti-fascist Croats, so somebody like Tudjman himself who, before taking up politics, was a rather second-rate historian, Tudjman tried to push the numbers down, whereas of course Serb propagandists have tried to push the numbers up. Croat numbers go down, in the case of Tudjman, to as few as 30,000. And, of course, Serb numbers go up, in the case of Dedijer, for example, they go up to 700,000 at Jasenovac alone. Since Dedijer's death, propagandists have pushed the number up even further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A good guess would be that probably something like 60-80,000 people died at Jasenovac. It could not really have been more, because first of all it only operated early in the war, the Germans put an end to a large part -- and it was extremely basic, primitive sort of camp. It was not industrialised death, such as the Germans were capable of.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any other camps in that territory where Serbs perished, where Serbs were liquidated, run by the independent state of Croatia, and here I do not mean only Serbs but others as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there certainly were other such camps. Jasenovac was the most notorious but there were others, especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which, of course -- most of which was part of the independent state of Croatia. There were camps in Eastern Slavonia as well. As far as I know, they were not -- they did not operate on the scale as the most notorious ones, but I have to admit that I am ignorant of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But there were such camps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were such camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know, by any chance -- you said that there was -- that the fact that Tudjman did not mention Serbs in the constitution, that that affected the Serbs, but on the other hand you also mentioned the SANU Memorandum. You probably know that the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts never recognised that memorandum as its own document. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed it is true. The memorandum was only a draft, and the manner by which -- yes, a draft, and the manner by which it was published was highly irregular. It was obviously in the interests of -- yes, it was a stolen copy, but it was in the interests of one of the principal authors to have it published. But it had no official character.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the draft of Franjo Tudjman, deleting the Serbs from the official constitution, was that of an official nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That certainly was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I am saying this, I am asking this, because the Defence will propose that you see a tape as to what happened to Serbs, I mean, in Jesenovaz, during the war. Since you know that a referendum was held on the status of Serbs, are you aware of the results of the referendum on the territory of the municipality of the Vukovar? Did they declare themselves in favour of remaining within Yugoslavia, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a referendum when?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The referendum that was held by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In August of 1990? I do not know what the result in Vukovar itself was. This of course -- as long as we are talking about whether things were official and unofficial, the Serb referendum of August 1990 took place over several days. Only Serbs were allowed to participate and it was highly unofficial. But I do not know the result in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, Croats took part in the referendum that was carried out by the Croats, and the referendum that was carried out by the Serbs -- it was Serbs who participated in it, is that right? But the results were different. One was in favour of the independent state of Croatia and the others were in favour of remaining within Yugoslavia. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not really possible to equate the two referenda, although -- I mean, in a legal sense, because the Republic of Croatia had an official referendum on 19th May 1991, regarding independence, in which all citizens of Croatia were eligible to vote. The Serbs had, in the summer of 1990, an unofficial referendum organised by themselves in which only Serbs were allowed to express their feelings about their continuation in the Yugoslav state.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you accept that the Serbs, just like the Croats, were constituent people of the state of Croatia. Then they have the same rights, both one and the other. Now let us move on to Vukovar. We will not agree on this. That is quite obvious. You said that the JNA was arming the Serbs, and the Territorial Defence of the Serbs and the Croatian Territorial Defence was disarmed so Croatia did not have any weapons. Who armed Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
