utterances.text: Well, Croatian forces, Croatian police were -- the police were distrusted by Tudjman when he came to power, and of course Croatia had no armed forces of its own, but certainly from the summer of 1990 tremendous efforts were made, particularly by the Croatian Defence Minister, Martin Spegelj, to acquire arms, and the Croatian regime bought arms everywhere it possibly could, and engaged in rather imaginative --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Hungary, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mostly in Hungary. There was a lot of arms flowing around in eastern Europe at the time, after the demise of the Warsaw Pact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At that point in time, was Croatia an integral part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the second half of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, when Croatia started importing arms, when the Spegelj affair broke out and when the trial was held in Zagreb. You remember that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gun-running was all taking place in the second half of 1990. The film exposing Spegelj was broadcast in January of 1991, so the principal arms activity was taking place, arms import activity was taking place --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between June and December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And was Croatia a part of the Yugoslav Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: According to the SFRY constitution which you read, are republics allowed to import and smuggle arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. The last time I asked you about the outcome of the Croatian referendum in Vukovar, we mentioned the Serb referendum, and what about the Croatian referendum in Vukovar? How did it fare? What did the population of Vukovar say in the Croatian referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I do not know the figures for Vukovar. The overall result for Croatia I do not know, but I do not know how the vote went in Vukovar. Given the former Communists, the Party of Democratic Change had won the 1990 elections in Vukovar, I would assume that sentiment in favour of independent Croatia may have been slightly less overwhelming in Vukovar. It was overwhelming once.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now let us move on to the actual situation there. Since you know the history there, whose army was the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a very good question. By the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. The Yugoslav army is an army without a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yugoslav People's Army. When it was established, whose army was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when it was established it was the army of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. There is no doubt about that. In 1991 the problem is that the army is looking for a new state to serve, because the old one has died.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The question remains when it ceased to exist, but at any rate, do you know when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was formed? Do you know when it was formally established and when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was founded, and I am a citizen of that country, by the way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not formally established until the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, did it have an army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The JNA? Is it the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the JNA no longer exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is what I was interested in. At the point when Vukovar was happening, do you know what the national composition, the ethnic composition of the JNA was in the fighting around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately, yes. About the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Percentage-wise -- no, sorry, I interrupted you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What had happened, of course, is that after the JNA incursion into Slovenia and the general trend of political developments, there was a massive desertion on the part of non-Serbs from the JNA, so that by the time the battles begin around Vukovar, the JNA is overwhelmingly Serb in composition. In other words, Slovenes are not there any more, Croats are not there any more, Macedonians are leaving in large numbers. I assume that there was a large desertion rate amongst "kosovars" as well, so both in terms of the officer core but also amongst the ranks of conscripts. The army had by that time, in other words, by the autumn of 1991, become an almost exclusively Serb force.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Have you heard of General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where is he from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Kadijevic is a product of a mixed marriage, Serb mother and Croat father, or the other way around. He is from Croatia, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Admiral Brovet? Was he a Serb, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Admiral Brovet is a Slovene.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So there were some Slovenes in the JNA, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what was the office that Admiral Brovet held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was Deputy Chief of Staff, I believe, or Deputy Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If a -- that is right. If a Slovene was the deputy head of general staff, that meant that there were some Slovenes in the army. Were there some Croats, perhaps? Do you want me to give you the names of officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not want to argue --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Exist even until the present? I am just asking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed they do exist. Individuals were confronted with absolutely horrible choices about where their loyalties lay, and obviously in many cases, officers -- especially high ranking officers, because I mean, an awful lot of nonsense has been talked about the extent to which the JNA were sort of dominated. At the highest levels it was extremely multinational, because it operated according to the so-called "kljuc" or the so-called ethnic key, so there was a fair proportion of Slovenes, Croats. Not of Albanians, it has to be said, but of Slovenes and Croats at the very top of the army, and these people whose careers, whose privileges, whose whole ideologies, their whole sense of themselves, was tied up in the army, they were in a horrible position, and many of them chose to remain loyal to their institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Muslim officers and Macedonian officers and soldiers, were they still there at the time or, to put it better, soldiers from Bosnia-Herzegovina, not to mention them specifically as Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were ever fewer, because in all Republics, including Serbia, as the war developed, more and more young men were refusing to be conscripted, and if they were in the army they were leaving very fast. One of the reasons why the JNA found it so difficult to take Vukovar, and one of the reasons it pursued the sort of battle it did, seeking to destroy the city with artillery rather than simply overrun it with infantry, was because it was so short of manpower, and so fearful that the manpower it did possess was not loyal, and had suffered with the decline and fall of Yugoslavia itself, a catastrophic fall in morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the time of the struggle for Vukovar, was there a presidency of the SFRY, and who was on the presidency if it existed in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In November 1991, the presidency -- the federal presidency effectively ceased to operate when Mesic was not -- did not rotate into the presidential chair on 15th May 1991. Eventually, for reasons to do with the international community's insistence that Brioni, that Mesic, Stipe Mesic, the Croat, should succeed to the presidency. He became nominally the president of the presidency, but he was hardly ever in Belgrade. It would have been extremely unsafe for him to have been in Belgrade. The presidency only existed fictionally, not in reality. So if, effectively, the Yugoslav People's Army was without any titular constitutional command. Mr. Kostic was really running the presidency, regardless of Mesic's supposed chairmanship of the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was on the presidency? Was Tupurkovski so the fighting for Vukovar started in August onwards. Was there a representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but Tupurkovski, and I assume Bogicevic, all stopped going to presidential meetings in the course of the autumn, just as gradually Ante Markovic abandoned his federal premiership. This was a very, very difficult period and chaotic from the point of view of sort of constitutional niceties.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At that time, one can say, then, that Ante Markovic was Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, who was coming and who was not coming, but in nominal terms he was Prime Minister, right? And at that time did Mesic say that he was coming to assume that office so that he would break up Yugoslavia, that he would be the last president of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stipe Mesic said that, certainly, in his memoirs, and I believe he is quoted to that effect in the press. The only time that Stipe Mesic actually tried during this period to exercise his presidential functions was when he was at the head of an armada of ferries, "trijakde", going down in to try and relieve the siege of Dubrovnik in the autumn of 1991 and he claimed, speaking to Stane Brovet on the telephone, that he was commanding the navy, to let his armada through to relieve Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did Croats start leaving their offices in the presidency? Do you know exactly when? Your Honour, all of that will be within the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They gradually left. I mean, Markovic formally resigned in December. Stipe Mesic did not attend any more presidential meetings after one that I think had to take place in September, but the reason why non-Serbs remained in these federal institutions was largely the insistence of the international community, that they should have some residual, recognised Yugoslav state with which to negotiate. It was, in other words, for international purposes, rather than because the federal institutions were any longer functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Finally, I will conclude by asking you two more questions. According to the 1974 constitution, was the right of peoples to self-determination formulated or of republics? Peoples or republics? The right to self-determination up to secession, or was it prohibited, this right? Was there a theory that it was taken advantage of once, and that that was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commonest theory, of course, was that it had been taken advantage of once, that at Jajce in November 29th 1943 it had happened, that that was the exercise of national self-determination. This was the second meeting of the anti-fascist council of national liberation in the Bosnian town of Jajce. Now, according to the letter of 1974 constitution, the prologue or the introduction does repeat the right of peoples, "naroda".

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. Not Republics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The right to self-determination, including and up to secession, belongs to the nations, not to the Republics. This is a very odd -- if I might add, this is very odd, given the fact that the entire purport, the entire thrust of the 1974 constitution, in fact, was to empower Republics rather than peoples or nations, but it happens, in this case, Mr. Fila is correct in his implication.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we agree that Serbs are a people too and that they had that same right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. When were republican boundaries first mentioned within the SFRY? Because we stopped when we mentioned Banovina, so let us bring this to a conclusion and then when the republican boundaries were established was there some referenda, or did Communists draw these boundaries at their own discretion? In other words, are these boundaries one of the reasons of this senseless bloodshed that occurred in our country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, arguments over boundaries have certainly become one of the reasons for the bloodshed that has taken place over the past seven years, but there is a real problem in talking about the republican boundaries. The problem stems from the fact that in a sense, because, as I indicated before in answer to Mr. Niemann, the Communists did not take the republican system in 1946, 45-46 very seriously. It was a national sentiment, rather than any sort of real national power. In other words, the Communists took very seriously indeed the symbolic importance of boundaries, so the boundaries were almost invariably founded on extremely sound historical or ethnographic bases, so the boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for example, are the historic boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina with, in fact, one unusual exception, and that is that in Turkish times, Bosnia had actually had a tiny outlet on to the Bay of Kotor. They lost that in 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: They lost Sandjak too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Sandjak was actually in a different category, but there were a series of gains and losses. Croatia, since we are interested in the area around Vukovar, Croatia lost Western Srem. That was given to Serbia both on ethnographic grounds, that the predominant population was Serbian, but it was also sensible on geographic grounds to add it to Vojvodina. So there was a violation of historical precedent there on the basis of ethnography and economic rationality. By the same token, Croatia got Baranja then. Baranja had never been part of Croatia, so as Croatia loses Western Srem, gets Baranja. It had effectively been part of Serbia before. So it is a mixture of historical and ethnographic reasons behind the boundaries. There were lots of fights and discussions -- I should not say, "fights" -- there were lots of arguments and discussions over them. For example, for our purposes today, the most interesting one was over Ilok, and that little salient which Milovan Dilas has insisted in the end that Croatia should get, because there was a big disagreement between the Communist parties of Vojvodina, Srem and Croatia generally about that part of the world, but -- so there were disputes about boundaries. There were all kinds of proposals for different autonomous areas. Pijade, Mose Pijade, one of the Communist leaders, had seriously suggested in the Second World War that there should be an autonomous Serb area in Croatia, and in fact it was highly likely until very late in the war that Sandjak would have been a republic, because Sandjak had its own anti-fascist council, so these things are all in flux, but they were simultaneously very important and simultaneously insignificant at the time. Insignificant because the Communists were determined that it really would not matter, but important because they were symbolic of the affirmation of the separate Yugoslav nations' identities which the Communists were seeking to promote. But the subsequent 1980s Serb version of reality, that somehow Serbia had been especially penalised, especially victimised, was a gross exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The point of this question was the following; were these boundaries treated as administrative boundaries or did the people have their democratic say in 1945 and 1946 as to where they would live? For example, if this means anything to you, there was never a boundary drawn between Serbia and Macedonia, and that is why there are problems today, because the parliaments of Serbian Macedonia did not ratify this. But this is a different question altogether. So, did the people have a democratic say of their own, where they would live and what side of the border, et cetera, I mean under the Communists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was understood through the "ovnoj" process that they had. I mean, in theory they had, in practice they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. If you recall, half were not in ovnoj. Just a few more questions -- but, well, formally speaking, Serbia, as one of the republics in the SFRY, did it have any jurisdiction under the JNA and the Territorial Defence in Croatia, and Territorial Defence generally speaking? Formally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Formally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. And the territory of Serbia, was a decision ever passed to annex any one of these territories of the former Yugoslavia to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not. They sought to annex themselves to Serbia, but Serbia did not accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did any official institution in Serbia, including the president of Serbia, Milosevic, officially ask for this kind of annexation? I am not talking about what was in Milosevic's mind, but officially.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in the period we are talking about. In fact, the first time that the autonomous region of Knin proclaimed its union with Serbia, Milosevic was widely reported to have been extremely annoyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Right. There is a large group of questions pertaining to local self-government and I do not think that I have enough time today. I would just confine myself to one further question today. During the so-called "Balvan revolution", the "logs revolution", as it was called colloquially, what was the attitude of the Croat population towards JNA barracks? We are going to discuss this in detail tomorrow because in JNA barracks, you will agree with that, I imagine, members of all nationalities were present, because we only have conscripts, we do not have professional soldiers in the army. Right? So, I am asking you kindly about that, rather I shall be questioning you about that tomorrow, about local self-government. You know, self-management, this wonder conceived by communism, so what the organisation of municipalities was et cetera, et cetera, so it is not related to this trial, but I should mention that I am not a Communist but I had to live in that system. My time is up, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will continue, you will continue with your cross-examination of our expert witness tomorrow morning. Before we adjourn I would like to thank you, Mr. Fila, for being so kind as to comply with my request that we should start today with the cross-examination. I wonder whether I could ask the Prosecutor whether, and how many witnesses he would like to call tomorrow ?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Two more witnesses tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry, are those the two people from Ilok? May I just know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, both from Ilok, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Thank you very much. I just want to prepare myself for that. (1.15 pm)
